p: Every Englishman believes that tea is as English as the Book of Common Prayer. It is a little over two hundred years since anyone in England drank it. Samuel Pepys, the diarist, recorded on the twenty-fifth of September, sixteen sixty, that he sent for a cup of tee, as he spelt it, a China drink, of which he had never drunk before. Within a century it was the drink of the whole nation, from duchesses to labourers. I can think of few better examples of the way in which a people may acquire, in a few generations, a habit which it then imagines it has always possessed. The history of mankind is full of such habits, and the most remarkable of them came in the wake of the voyages of discovery, when the products of every continent were suddenly available to every other.

Coffee comes from Ethiopia, where the berries of a wild shrub were chewed for their stimulating effect; the legend, of a goatherd named Kaldi who noticed his goats dancing after eating them, is recorded only very late and need not detain us. The drink, made from the roasted beans, appears first, the Encyclopaedia says, in the fifteenth century among the Sufi mystics of Yemen, who drank it to keep themselves awake through their night-long devotions. From Yemen it spread through the Islamic world, to Mecca, to Cairo, and to Constantinople, where the first coffee houses opened about fifteen fifty-five.

The coffee house was a new kind of institution: a public place where men of different ranks could meet, sit, talk, play chess, hear poetry and discuss the news, without the drunkenness of the tavern. That last point made it respectable; the first made it suspect. Rulers in the Ottoman Empire and elsewhere repeatedly tried to close the coffee houses as nests of sedition and idle gossip. They failed, as rulers have generally failed when they set themselves against a beverage.

The first coffee house in England was opened at Oxford in sixteen fifty, by a Jew named Jacob, at the sign of the Angel; I have myself drunk coffee within a few yards of the spot. London followed in sixteen fifty-two, and within fifty years there were hundreds. They were called penny universities, because for the price of a cup any man could listen to the conversation of the learned. Each had its own character and clientele. Lloyd's coffee house, frequented by sea captains and merchants, became the great house of marine insurance that bears the name to this day. The stock exchange grew from the coffee houses of Exchange Alley. The Royal Society's Fellows met in them, and Sir Isaac Newton, it is said, once dissected a dolphin on a coffee-house table. Writers such as Addison and Steele made them the setting of their essays in The Spectator. King Charles the Second, suspecting them of disaffection, issued a proclamation in sixteen seventy-five to suppress them, and withdrew it within eleven days in the face of public outrage. Some historians, especially a German philosopher of the twentieth century named Jürgen Habermas, have argued that the coffee houses created something new in European life, a public sphere, in which private persons came together to discuss public affairs, and that modern public opinion was born there. I am inclined to agree, having formed most of my own opinions in a coffee room.

Tea is far older, cultivated and drunk in China for at least two thousand years, and elevated there and in Japan into an art and a ceremony. It reached Europe through the Dutch early in the seventeenth century, and England through the marriage of King Charles the Second to a Portuguese princess, Catherine of Braganza, who brought the habit with her in sixteen sixty-two. The East India Company made it the foundation of its trade with China. By the eighteenth century the English drank so much of it, and the duties on it were so high, that it was smuggled on a vast scale. When the government in London tried to collect a tax on tea from the American colonists, they threw it into Boston harbour, with consequences I shall describe in their place. And because the Chinese wanted little that Britain made, and had to be paid in silver, the Company began to sell them opium grown in India, and when the Chinese government tried to stop the traffic, Britain made war on China, in eighteen thirty-nine and again in eighteen fifty-six. It is not a story in which my country appears to advantage. A nation's breakfast table may rest upon some very dark foundations.

Chocolate was the drink of the Aztec nobility, bitter and spiced with chilli, and the Spaniards, having learned to sweeten it with sugar, made it the fashionable drink of the courts of Europe in the seventeenth century. Tobacco, smoked by the peoples of America for many centuries in ceremonies and for pleasure, was brought to Europe in the sixteenth century, and spread through the whole world within a hundred years, to the Ottoman lands, to India, to China and to Japan, in spite of every effort to forbid it. King James the First wrote a pamphlet called A Counterblaste to Tobacco, describing smoking as a custom loathsome to the eye, hateful to the nose, harmful to the brain, dangerous to the lungs. The men of the future, I am told, have shown by careful measurement that he was right about the lungs, and that tobacco has killed many millions. The King, in the meantime, taxed it.

What do these new habits tell us? First, that the global trade of the modern age reached into every household, changing what people ate, drank and did with their leisure. Second, that a great part of that trade was in stimulants and luxuries, not necessities, and that these were grown largely by enslaved or coerced labour in distant lands, sugar above all, to be sweetened into every cup. And third, that new habits create new institutions: the coffee house, the tea table, the smoking room, each with its own manners, its own conversations, its own place in the life of a society. History is made not only in parliaments and on battlefields, but over the breakfast cup.
